items.t: GIS-Based Multi-Criteria Assessment of Hybrid  Solar-Wind Suitability in Maharashtra
items.x: A district-level planning atlas showing where hybrid solar–wind projects make sense across all 36 districts of Maharashtra at 100 m resolution, combining GIS-AHP, 30 years of climate data and pixel-level cost estimates. Certificate of Excellence in the "Infrastructure Readiness and System Reliability" track at Accelerating Clean Energy (ACE) 2026, organised by WRI India and GESH, IIT Bombay

sections.t: Maharashtra's renewable energy policy targets 100 GW by 2035–36, against about 31.7 GW today. Closing that gap depends on knowing where to build. Planners often rely on coarse 1 km global data, resource maps that ignore whether a site can beat the grid tariff, and studies that treat every month alike, even though the state's monsoon wind and summer solar tend to peak at different times.

The aim was a reproducible GIS-AHP framework mapping hybrid solar–wind suitability across all 36 districts at 100 m resolution. I first removed unsuitable land (slopes above 20°, forests, built-up areas, water bodies, wetlands and mangroves, and a 1 km buffer around protected areas), which excluded 30.7% of the state. I then scored the remaining land on six criteria weighted with the Analytic Hierarchy Process (consistency ratio 0.017): solar irradiance, wind speed, seasonal solar–wind complementarity, slope, grid proximity and road proximity.

Complementarity came from 30 years of ERA5 monthly data (1993–2023) using Spearman rank correlation, showing where solar and wind peak at different times of year. I also estimated pixel-level levelised cost of energy (LCOE) with CERC 2024 parameters, to test where projects beat the grid tariff and not only where the resource is strong.

About 45.3% of Maharashtra (139,324 km²) rates high or very high for hybrid development. Washim ranks first at district level, followed by Nashik, Nandurbar, Hingoli and Jalna. Mean solar LCOE is ₹3.09/kWh against a ₹6–8/kWh grid tariff, and no pixel exceeds ₹6/kWh. Competitive wind is confined to roughly 20% of the state, mainly the Western Ghats, which makes wind the main spatial differentiator, since solar resource is nearly uniform across the Deccan plateau.

I tested the map against 292 operating solar and wind plants (253 solar, 39 wind) from the Global Energy Monitor tracker, after removing 111 points that fell inside excluded zones. The AUC was 0.858, and 72.8% of the plants fall in the high or very high classes. Rankings stayed stable under three alternative weighting scenarios (Cohen's kappa 0.93–0.99 against the base case).

At 100 m, the atlas suits district-level planning but not turbine micro-siting. Monthly ERA5 data misses day–night cycles, so storage needs are not quantified, and tribal settlements, Forest Rights Act claims and community land are not mapped, so some high-suitability areas may overlap contested land. Next steps are hourly ERA5 analysis, a social exclusion layer, LCOE projections to 2030 and 2035, and extending the method to other states.

Best Research Presentation, Accelerating Clean Energy (ACE) 2026, Infrastructure Readiness and System Reliability track, organised by WRI India and GESH, IIT Bombay. Tools: QGIS, Google Earth Engine, Python (pandas, NumPy, rasterio, GeoPandas, SciPy, scikit-learn), Overpass Turbo and Excel.

items.t: Rural Fieldwork: Multidimensional Vulnerability in Dhundalwadi, Palghar
items.x: Four-day participatory fieldwork in a tribal, earthquake-affected village in Palghar, Maharashtra. We used qualitative interviews and GIS to profile livelihoods, health, food security, hazards and vulnerability.

sections.t: This fieldwork was carried out for course MDM-408 (Rural Fieldwork) at the Jamsetji Tata School of Disaster Studies, Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai. A group of five of us stayed in Dhundalwadi village, Palghar district, Maharashtra, for four days (26–29 November). Dhundalwadi was the epicentre of the 2019 earthquake swarm and still feels occasional tremors. The village is mainly tribal and sits next to Vedanta Hospital and MBBS College. Our task was to understand livelihood patterns, health, food security and social and economic vulnerabilities, and to examine the multidimensional poverty in the village.

We used participatory methods and detailed qualitative interviews with residents, government officials and technical experts to build the village profile. We created the village boundary and resource maps using GIS software, Google Earth Pro and SW Maps. The visit also showed us how access to resources differs across households, and how to work respectfully in a rural community setting.

Dhundalwadi falls under the Dhundalwadi Gram Panchayat, established on 19 May 1960, which also covers Pardi village. It has about 2,700 people living in eight paras: Patil, Dhodi, Kharki, Nauwa, Bazar, Kumar, Mumbai and Pardi. There are 237 Scheduled Tribe families, from the Kokna, Warli, Kadkari and Dhodi communities, and the Kokna are the largest group. Livelihoods depend mainly on agriculture and daily wage labour. Some shopkeepers have settled here from Rajasthan, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh. Services include two Anganwadis, two Zilla Parishad schools and a veterinary clinic near the Talathi office. The primary health centre was being rebuilt during our visit, so residents depended on nearby Vedanta Hospital. Many families hold Yellow, Orange or White ration cards, and many are covered by the Ladli Behna scheme.

Physical: electricity is inconsistent, drinking water comes mainly from hand pumps and wells, solid waste is disposed of informally, and poor roads limit access to markets, schools and healthcare. 

Economic: average household income is about ₹8,000–12,000 per month, agriculture and labour are the main livelihoods, and education levels are low with little access to higher education. Some residents work as hospital staff, teachers or shopkeepers. 

Social and political: caste, tribal identity and cultural diversity shape who takes part in community development, and many people have limited participation in local governance. The report calls for stronger inclusion and representation.

Environmental: informal waste disposal and agricultural runoff degrade water and soil quality. The village lies in an earthquake-prone zone, and deforestation and climate change add further risks. Health: a single primary health centre and two Anganwadis cannot meet community needs, and limited access to clean water worsens health outcomes. The report links this to waterborne disease and kidney problems among villagers. Strengthening healthcare, raising awareness and addressing water access are identified as priorities.

The map shows a dispersed settlement pattern, with homes and clusters spread across the village and linked by a network of main and internal roads. Dahanu Road connects Dhundalwadi to the Golden Quadrilateral Highway. Key economic and social hubs include a weekly market and an ashram school serving tribal children. The map also marks shops, banks, government buildings and religious places. Proximity to Dahanu and the highway gives the village development potential, and the report suggests improving internal roads, upgrading market facilities and expanding access to education and healthcare.

Earthquakes: the village is in Seismic Zone III (moderate risk). Mud-and-stone houses cannot withstand even minor tremors. A magnitude 4.1 tremor had its epicentre near the village on 1 February 2019, part of a swarm that began in late 2018. Residents, officials and technical experts told us that over 600 tremors were felt in 2018–19. Rumours linked the quakes to construction projects such as the bullet train and highways, while some experts attributed them to magma movement beneath the area. Drought: rain-fed farming leaves water for drinking and irrigation vulnerable to delayed or weak monsoons. Heatwaves: outdoor workers face heatstroke and dehydration, with few cooling facilities or nearby medical centres. Deforestation: clearing for farming and firewood affects tribal communities and traditional agricultural practices.

Provisioning: two major streams supply water, rice is the main food crop, and tadi trees are used for a local drink. Regulating: dependence on groundwater and rain makes rice farming vulnerable to drought, which has made people more aware of government-supported rationing programmes. Cultural: festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi and various tribal festivals, each with community-specific rituals, bring people together. 

Conclusion: despite the challenges, residents have shown strong resilience. The report recommends better roads, water systems and healthcare, along with sustainable agriculture, skill development and employment opportunities.
Anurag Tripathi, Ashutosh Gaurav, Binayak Maitra, Chandrakiran Gudipudi

items.t: Urban Fieldwork: Multidimensional Vulnerability in Jai Ambe Nagar, Chembur, Mumbai
items.x: Fieldwork in a largely migrant, low-income urban settlement in Chembur, Mumbai, to understand how poverty, weak infrastructure and environmental hazards combine to create vulnerability. The work used community profiling, GIS resource mapping and hazard and vulnerability assessment.

sections.t: This fieldwork was carried out for course MDM-408 (Urban Fieldwork) at the Jamsetji Tata School of Disaster Studies, TISS Mumbai. Jai Ambe Nagar in Chembur, Mumbai, is a largely migrant community, with residents mostly from Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka and Maharashtra. Residents deal with insecure employment, low wages and administrative neglect, living in overcrowded housing with inadequate electricity, clean water, sanitation and road connectivity. Water stagnation and the settlement’s closeness to a large drainage channel add serious health risks. The aim of the visit was to understand the systemic factors that sustain urban poverty and social exclusion, and to explore interventions that could improve quality of life.

The settlement is home to several communities, including the Masanyogi, Pardi, Warli and Rath communities, who face similar challenges. This is why the report argues for targeted interventions. Average household income is about ₹8,000–12,000 per month, and most livelihoods are informal, so income is unstable. Literacy is low, especially among women, and access to higher education is limited. Most houses are owned but poorly built.

Electricity is unreliable and outages are frequent. Many households depend on distant sources for drinking water. Sanitation is inadequate and open defecation is widespread. Homes are poorly built, with little ventilation and weak roofing, so they are exposed to environmental hazards. Waste is disposed of informally, and limited road connectivity restricts access to schools, hospitals and markets. There are no robust early warning systems or evacuation plans.

Economic: informal work gives unstable income, and very low earnings are likely to mean high household debt, though debt details were not available. 

Social: the community includes marginalised groups and migrants who face a risk of institutional exclusion. Religious, ethnic and linguistic diversity can be a barrier to social bonding and equal access to basic amenities, and weak community engagement limits collective decision-making. 

Political: democratic institutions are scarce, and these groups have little voice in decisions that affect them, which reduces their ability to advocate for resources.

Environmental: poor air and water quality, closeness to waste disposal areas and flood-prone zones, and the effects of rapid urbanisation and climate change raise existing risks. 

Health: a single Anganwadi cannot meet the health and nutrition needs of children and mothers. Cultural barriers and low literacy make people less likely to seek care. Poor hygiene and sanitation, lack of clean drinking water and poor nutrition make the community more prone to disease.

The map covers the layout, socio-economic features and infrastructure of Jai Ambe Nagar. The area is well connected by train and road, with boundaries running from a main thoroughfare in Chembur to the bypass road, and the Mumbai–Pune Highway lies nearby. Slum settlements house much of the population, and their elevated position protects them from monsoon waterlogging. Housing is diverse, ranging from informal dwellings to more structured homes. Local shops serve daily needs, and two NGOs, Smile and Saman, work with disadvantaged residents. The nearby drainage sewer and highway bring pollution and health risks. The report recommends better sanitation, hazard mitigation near the highway and sewer, housing upgrades, and development planning that builds on local knowledge and NGO support.

Flooding: heavy monsoon rain, sewage overflow and wetland encroachment cause flooding, and the stagnant water breeds mosquitoes and contaminates water sources, raising malaria, dengue and waterborne disease. Earthquakes: the area carries a significant risk, which could damage infrastructure and jhuggis. Heatwaves: urbanisation, limited green cover, tightly packed housing and metal-sheet roofs worsen heat stress, especially for children, older adults and outdoor workers. Structural collapse: temporary materials such as tarpaulin, wood and metal sheets collapse easily in extreme weather without maintenance. Pollution: industrial emissions, traffic, poor waste management and the nearby sewer degrade air and water. Fire: dense housing, electrical short circuits and poorly stored combustible material threaten lives and property. Pandemics: high density, weak healthcare and low hygiene awareness helped infectious diseases spread, and preparedness was inadequate.

Using the Pressure and Release (PAR) model, the report shows how poverty, exclusion and environmental degradation reinforce each other. Residents rely on daily-wage informal work. Repeated demolitions and a lack of affordable housing push families into fragile, overcrowded homes. Rapid unplanned growth has left electricity, water and sanitation inadequate, with open defecation reported as very widespread. Stagnant water and a large nala nearby raise the risk of cholera and dengue. Women and youth carry added burdens, and limited education and jobs trap many young people in informal work. The report concludes that these problems come from a system that has failed its residents, and that breaking the cycle needs sustained work on housing, sanitation and health, plus education and employment opportunities. It also stresses the community’s resilience.
Anurag Tripathi, Ashutosh Gaurav, Binayak Maitra, Chandrakiran Gudipudi

items.t: Belapur Village Fieldwork: Participatory Risk Assessment and Ecosystem-Based DRR Planning, Navi Mumbai
items.x: A 21-day field practicum (April–May 2025) in Belapur Village (gaothan) and the Belapur Node, Navi Mumbai, on mainstreaming disaster risk reduction into development planning. The work used participatory HRVA, ecosystem and land-use mapping, and engagement with NMMC departments, and produced a village disaster management plan, a development plan and a node-level report.

sections.t: This 21-day field practicum at the Jamsetji Tata School of Disaster Studies, TISS Mumbai, was carried out in April–May 2025 by a group of five students. It explored how DRR can be mainstreamed into development planning through an ecosystem-based approach. We drew on coursework in Ecosystems and Habitat, Policy Institutions and Governance, and Disasters and Development. The study area was Belapur Village (the gaothan) in the Belapur Node, Navi Mumbai. Our objectives were to hold participatory hazard, vulnerability and risk assessments (HRVA) with residents, map ecosystem services (mangroves, wetlands, hill slopes) and land-use change, engage government officials to understand institutional processes, and critically review the development and disaster management plans at village and node levels.

We compared five villages in the node (Belapur, Diwale, Shahbaz, Agroli and Phanaspada) on ecological sensitivity, urbanisation pressure, ecosystem-based DRR potential, community engagement potential and the urban–ecological interface. Belapur stood out for its dense mangroves, nullahs and Parsik Hills, rapid encroachment, visible ecosystem services such as flood buffering and cooling, and strong Koli–Agri community networks. It is a former Koli–Agri settlement turned urban fringe, where CIDCO land acquisition, wetland filling from the 1990s and roads built over nullahs have altered drainage. The village and the planned CBD sit side by side, which made it a good place to study the conflict between hill, wetland and dense housing.

Before fieldwork we reviewed Belapur’s Comprehensive Development Plan, mapped historical flood hotspots from archived news, adapted participatory HRVA tools, and held a roundtable with Navi Mumbai’s Town Planning Department. In the field we surveyed 36 households at random on hazard exposure, vulnerability and coping, and held focus group discussions with elders, fisherfolk, women and youth. We also conducted key informant interviews with the ward officer, PHC staff and forest ranger, and transect walks with GPS mapping across creek edges, gaothan lanes and hill slopes. Participatory tools included social mapping, hazard ranking and resource mapping, and a stakeholder influence–interest matrix. For secondary analysis we processed Landsat imagery in QGIS and Google Earth Engine for land use and land cover, NDVI and NDWI, and used Census 2011 and NMMC documents. The household HRVA gave an overall community vulnerability index of 0.44.

Participatory mapping let residents identify flood-prone lanes, blocked drains and non-engineered structures, and coping resources such as temples, public wells, fishing boats and open grounds for evacuation. Women-only walks surfaced water points that men did not mention. We also worked with school students on resource mapping. We met NMMC’s Town Planning, Health, Water Supply, Stormwater Drainage, Electricity, Parks and Fire departments, the Forest Department’s mangrove conservation officers, and the Ward Officer. These meetings covered zoning and hazard data in the CDP, seasonal disease outbreaks, fire safety in narrow lanes, encroachment on mangroves, and how coordination, budgets and complaints work at ward level. Language barriers with elderly residents and work schedules limited participation at first. We used Marathi-speaking students as facilitators, built rapport informally, and met youth in the evenings.

The Belapur Node covers 9.68 km² (30 sectors) on Navi Mumbai’s creek edge and hillslope, from tidal flats at about 3 m above sea level to Parsik Hill at 305 m. It combines the planned CBD, a showcase of high-rise offices and apartments, with the much older Belapur Village, a dense fishing settlement. Population grew from about 65,000 in 2011 to about 134,000 in 2024, and about 51% of the node is developed. From the 1970s CIDCO’s planned grid replaced paddy fields and marshland. Meanwhile the village grew informally, with cottages becoming G+3 rentals, lanes narrowing and mangrove fringes landfilled for parking. This planned–unplanned divide drives unequal exposure to hazards.

The node’s mangroves, tidal marshes and holding ponds buffer tidal energy, trap sediment, store monsoon runoff, recharge aquifers and sustain fisheries for the Koli and Agri communities. The node report estimates that these ecosystems attenuate tidal energy by up to 80% and sequester about 1,200 t of CO₂ a year. Our change-detection analysis showed about 4.9% of mangrove wetland cover lost between 2000 and 2020, and saltpans shrinking from 315 ha to 112 ha. Land-use classification, false-colour composites (1992, 2013, 2025), NDVI and NDWI showed rising built-up area, patchy vegetation, and shrinking ponds and drying streambeds before the monsoon. Successive development plans earmarked land for parks, sewage plants and holding ponds. Later revisions diluted forest reservations, and a proposed 35 km coastal road would cut through mangrove belts.

Using a likelihood–impact matrix, we ranked five dominant hazards. Urban flooding and waterlogging (almost certain) come from poor drainage, silting of the Sector 12 holding pond and heavy rain, with hotspots in the creek-side gaothan, Sectors 1–3 and the pond zone. Fire and heatwaves (likely) affect congested lanes, tin-roof homes and the concrete CBD core. Building collapse (possible) is a risk in older and unauthorised gaothan structures. Landslides and hillside runoff (possible) threaten the Parsik Hill slopes. Vulnerability was assessed across social, economic, physical and governance dimensions. High-risk groups include the elderly, children, women, people with disabilities, daily-wage earners and migrants. Gaps include open drains, informal housing, limited fire access and no active village DRR committee. Capacities include the PHC, youth groups, fisherfolk, SHGs and religious institutions as informal support networks.

sections.h: Village Disaster Management and Development Plan
sections.t: Our village DM plan follows the Sendai Framework and NDMA village guidelines. Mitigation covers drainage flaps against tidal backflow, desilting, structural audits and retrofitting, wiring checks, mangrove restoration and tree planting, and fogging and waste management. Preparedness includes a Disaster Management Committee of volunteers, ASHAs, SHGs and teachers, bi-annual mock drills, early warning through WhatsApp groups, megaphones and sirens, emergency stocks, and wall art and school programmes for awareness. The response plan makes the Ward Officer Incident Commander, with evacuation of low-lying areas within two hours to schools and community halls, and a GIS evacuation-road map. Recovery includes joint damage assessment within 48 hours, relief with trauma care, and rebuilding using SDRF funds, micro-loans and cash-for-work. The development plan proposes no-development zones along the creek, micro-zoning, safe and affordable housing, better water, sanitation and drainage, livelihood support for fisherfolk and informal workers, and wetland, creek and hill-slope protection.

Governance and equity: CIDCO, NMMC and the Forest Department overlap, causing “multiple authority confusion” that delays maintenance and wetland restoration permits. Service quality is uneven: CBD towers have full piped water, while slum rows rely on intermittent standposts and 47 community toilets serve over 15,000 gaothan residents. Women report safety concerns in dimly lit lanes, and women’s representation in ward committees is under 15%. Reflections: development can amplify risk, with built-over water channels turning ordinary rain into waterlogging. Plans on paper often fail in implementation, and many residents lacking documents miss welfare schemes. Residents already craft their own solutions, such as shared water hoses, rooftop gardens and women’s SHG nutrition tips. 

Recommendations: restore natural buffers by desilting ponds and fencing mangroves, extend services and early warning into inner lanes, enforce and subsidise safety retrofits, create a Belapur Node Resilience Cell convening CIDCO, NMMC, the Forest Department and NGOs, and reserve seats for women and SC/ST representatives in ward-level DM committees.
Ashutosh Gaurav, Hemant Paliwal, Jessica Christine Soreng, Chandrakiran Gudipudi

items.t: Integrated Spatial and Economic Valuation of Urban Wetlands for Climate Resilient Planning (Nagpur)
items.x:
M.Sc. Disaster Management dissertation, Jamsetji Tata School of Disaster Studies, Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai. 

Supervisor: Ms. Niti Mishra. 

Abstract: Urban wetlands in Indian cities are rarely valued in planning decisions. This study quantifies the cooling services and wider ecosystem benefits of Nagpur’s wetlands by combining remote sensing, landscape connectivity analysis, ward-level equity mapping and cost-benefit analysis. It values four priority wetlands at ₹123.93 crore a year and shows that ecological restoration returns a benefit-cost ratio of 1.9 to 10.2, well above roads and drains. It also proposes a decision tool, the Integrated Wetland Investment Index, for prioritising conservation spending.

sections.t: Urban wetlands in rapidly growing Indian cities face heavy development pressure, yet their ecological and economic value is rarely quantified, so they are “economically invisible” in planning decisions. Nagpur is a Tier-2 city with summer temperatures regularly above 45°C and a strong Urban Heat Island effect. Its wetland cover fell by about 60% between 2000 and 2024 (from 10.9 km² to 4.3 km²), and at least eight wetlands were lost to landfilling. The thesis treats the Urban Heat Island as a severe, slow-onset climate hazard that disaster management frameworks tend to overlook. It sets out to give municipal planners usable financial and spatial evidence to defend wetland conservation against competing grey infrastructure projects.

The study covers the Nagpur Municipal Corporation area (about 227 km², roughly 2.8–3.0 million people) and its municipal wards. A total of 36 water features were mapped: 21 wetlands and lakes covering about 359 ha (1.67% of the study area) and 15 river and stream segments totalling 70 km. Four priority wetlands were studied in detail, chosen to vary in size, condition and position on the urban to peri-urban gradient: Ambazari (the network anchor), Gorewada (a peri-urban forest-edge wetland), Futala (an urban-core lake) and Gandhisagar (a small, deep lake in the old city). The framework is directly relevant to the Smart Cities Mission and AMRUT, including Ambazari’s Smart Cities designation and Gandhisagar’s proposed AMRUT restoration.

Objectives: 
(1) identify, classify and map urban and peri-urban wetlands in a Tier-2 city 
(2) evaluate their spatial cooling performance
(3) assess their ecological importance and role in landscape connectivity 
(4) assess their socio-economic value by balancing benefits and costs 
(5) build a decision-support framework combining ecological, thermal and economic dimensions. 

The research questions ask how wetlands can be identified from satellite imagery, how strongly they cool the city, how connected they are, whether wetland-based green-blue infrastructure is economically viable, and how these indicators can be combined to prioritise wetlands for climate-resilient planning.

This is a mixed quantitative design with descriptive, analytical and comparative parts. Data came from Landsat 8 (land surface temperature on 29 May 2024, during an IMD-confirmed severe heat wave), ESRI Sentinel-2 land cover for 2024, wetlands digitised from Google Earth Pro imagery, NASA POWER meteorological data for validation, Census 2011 ward data and municipal cost records. The workflow runs from land use and land cover classification to land surface temperature retrieval, wetland mapping, Morphological Spatial Pattern Analysis (MSPA) and graph-based connectivity modelling in Conefor (1,000 m dispersal threshold). Cooling was measured with distance-decay analysis in concentric 30 m buffers out to 2,000 m. Ward-level analysis used a Wetland Influence Score, a Heat Vulnerability Index and K-means clustering. Valuation used six monetised ecosystem services and three benefit-cost models with a 10% discount rate and 2024 prices, following NITI Aayog guidance.

sections.h: Land Cover and the Urban Heat Island
sections.t: Built-up area covers 77% of Nagpur (165.58 km²), vegetation only 3% and water bodies 2%. Between 2000 and 2024, built-up area rose by 35.76% and vegetation fell by 21.17%. On 29 May 2024 land surface temperature ranged from 26.08°C (over water) to 47.63°C (dense urban areas), with a mean of 38.85°C. Built-up surfaces averaged 41.79°C against about 35.8°C for the rural baseline, an urban–rural difference of about 6°C. Water bodies were the strongest cooling agent, 14.37°C below built-up surfaces. Dense vegetation cooled by 7.23°C, croplands by 4.67°C and rangeland by 2.55°C.

MSPA and probabilistic connectivity modelling show a network of moderate overall connectivity (PC = 0.54, IIC = 0.42) built around two hubs. Ambazari makes up 35.3% of wetland area but accounts for 55.7% of network connectivity, and removing it would cut overall connectivity by 67.6% and split the network into three parts. Gorewada is the secondary hub, acting as a habitat anchor. Futala is the key distribution node for connectivity flow despite being much smaller. The eastern wetlands are isolated, and several structural bottlenecks need corridors. The network is efficient but fragile, depending heavily on a few hubs.

Wetlands and the vegetation around them lowered surface temperature measurably, and cooling reached up to about 390 m from the edge. Wetland area correlates strongly with cooling intensity (r = 0.758), and shape also matters: more complex, irregular outlines cool less. Regression models explained most of the variation in cooling intensity (R² = 0.76) and in the combined Wetland Cooling Index (R² = 0.87), while cooling extent was harder to predict (R² = 0.15). Futala was the thermal performance leader on the Wetland Cooling-Ecosystem Service Index (0.793), followed by Gorewada (0.786), Gandhisagar (0.767) and Ambazari (0.720).

A Wetland Influence Score (WIS) for each ward ranged from 0.005 to 0.751. Ten wards (29%) were “cooling deserts” with a very low score, leaving about 617,000 people without cooling benefits, mainly in the eastern and south-western periphery and the northern industrial belt. Ward 20 scored highest, benefiting from Gandhisagar, Futala and Ambazari. K-means clustering produced four thermal types, including “Heat Trapped, Cooling Deprived” wards about 3.1°C above the city mean and “Cool and Connected” wards near wetlands. A three-tier plan prioritises 8 wards (about 493,000 people) for urgent intervention, 9 for strategic enhancement and 21 for protection. In Ward 12, the hottest, 14.2 ha of vacant land could host micro-wetlands that raise its score from 0.008 to above 0.28. The hot, wetland-poor wards also overlap with low-income informal settlements.

Six services were monetised: urban cooling, flood regulation, carbon sequestration, water purification, biodiversity support and recreation. Together the four priority wetlands are worth ₹123.93 crore per year: Ambazari ₹52.73 crore, Futala ₹25.71 crore, Gorewada ₹24.52 crore and Gandhisagar ₹20.97 crore. Urban cooling (₹56.63 crore, 45.7%) and flood regulation (₹45.27 crore, 36.5%) make up over 82% of the total, so the value lies mainly in climate adaptation. Ambazari’s value is dominated by flood regulation, Gandhisagar’s by cooling (80% of its total) and Gorewada’s by biodiversity and recreation. Carbon sequestration is the smallest share (0.27%). Estimates are conservative and use benefit transfer from Indian wetland studies, with a ±30% sensitivity range.

Each wetland was assessed over a 30-year life at a 10% discount rate, comparing an “ecological core” scenario with a “full system” that adds amenities. Model 1 (true system) gives benefit-cost ratios of 10.15 for Ambazari, 3.63 for Futala Core, 3.15 for Gandhisagar and 1.90 for Gorewada Core. The full-system versions fall to 1.41 for Futala and 0.51 for Gorewada, because items like the zoo (about ₹312 crore) and a musical fountain add cost without adding ecosystem services. For Futala this cut the ratio by 61% and stretched payback from 4.2 to 13.4 years. A capacity-adjusted Model 2 is the main decision model, and a project counts as viable only if both it and the worst-case stress test exceed 1.0. All four ecological core scenarios pass. Payback is 0.7–5.2 years, compared with about 14 years for the Outer Ring Road (BCR 1.28) and 18.6 years for the Nag River drain (BCR 1.05). Wetlands therefore return roughly 1.5 to 7.9 times the benefit-cost ratio of the grey infrastructure used for comparison.

Five indices combine the thermal, connectivity and economic results: the Wetland Cooling-Ecosystem Service Index (WC-ESI), the Integrated Wetland Connectivity Index (IWCI), the Urban Wetland Multifunctionality Index (UWMFI), the Cooling-Connectivity Coupling Coordination Index (CCCI) and the Cooling Resilience Index (CRI). They feed the Integrated Wetland Investment Index (IWII), which also uses a normalised benefit-cost score and a ward equity modifier. IWII scores are Ambazari 0.576 and Futala 0.514 (both Tier 2), Gorewada 0.483 and Gandhisagar 0.418 (Tier 3). Single-criterion ranking can mislead. Ranking by area alone would place Gandhisagar 15th of 21 wetlands, yet it is the only heatwave cooling refuge for Ward 20 (about 18,200 people). Ranking by benefit-cost ratio alone would call Gorewada non-viable and ignore its role as a forest-wetland biodiversity corridor with 87 bird species. Ranking by connectivity alone would put about 75% of the budget into Ambazari.

Protect and invest according to each wetland’s profile. Ambazari’s main weakness is its irregular, encroached edge (shape index 2.30 along a 9.99 km perimeter), so removing encroachments is the priority. Futala is the best candidate for concessional finance such as the Green Climate Fund or NABARD, which could cut capital costs by 40–60%. Gandhisagar’s 5 m depth should be protected, since dredging it to 3.5–4.0 m could cut cooling efficiency by 32–42%, raise Ward 20’s heat vulnerability from 0.31 to 0.48–0.56 and cost ₹56–85 crore. Gorewada needs ecological corridors, including a ₹8.06 crore Ash Pond extension, and its zoo costs should be separated from conservation costs. Tier 1 wards need micro-wetlands, tree cover and emergency cooling centres within 3 years. Tier 3 wards such as 30 and 13 should be notified as Ecologically Sensitive Zones under the Wetlands Rules 2017 with no-development zones.

Limitations: the thermal analysis rests on a single Landsat scene (29 May 2024), so seasonal cooling is not captured; thermal data at 100 m resolution (resampled to 30 m) blur small wetlands below about 0.5 ha; values come from benefit transfer, not primary surveys of Nagpur residents; equity data are from Census 2011; index weights reflect analytical judgement, not stakeholder input; and the 1,000 m dispersal threshold is generic, not species-specific. Way forward: scale the framework across India’s Tier-2 cities through a national wetland assessment network; add IoT sensors for live monitoring; include social, environmental justice and cultural dimensions; train machine learning models across cities; and build a web-based decision-support platform for planners. Future work should use multi-season thermal data, resident surveys for valuation, participatory weighting with ward officers and communities, and updated 2026 Census data.

The thesis argues that urban wetlands are critical urban infrastructure that cools neighbourhoods, absorbs floodwater and supports biodiversity, not leftover land to be built over. It offers what the author describes as the first localised, evidence-based economic valuation of wetland ecosystem services for an Indian Tier-2 city, and a replicable method that links satellite thermal analysis, landscape connectivity, equity mapping and cost-benefit analysis. Nagpur’s wetlands cover less than 2% of the urban footprint yet deliver about ₹124 crore a year in services. The work moves wetland planning from “wetlands versus development” toward investing in wetlands as development.

items.t: Mitigating Extreme Heat in Maharashtra (2025): Evaluating Wada Architecture as a Sustainable Cooling Measure
items.x: As air conditioning is unaffordable for most households, this article looks at the Wada, a traditional Maratha and Peshwa-era house with courtyards, thick walls, verandahs and jaali screens. Studies cited in the piece report that Wadas stay about 4–6°C cooler than outdoor temperatures and use around 40% less cooling energy than modern housing. It argues that retrofitted Wadas should be treated as living climate adaptation, not relics.

items.t: Urban Heat Island: Strategies for Mitigating the Effects in India
items.x: Indian cities like Delhi, Ahmedabad, Nagpur and Hyderabad regularly pass 45°C, and the urban heat island effect turns heatwaves into public health emergencies. This piece argues for green and blue infrastructure such as wetlands, urban forests and street trees. Global evidence shows these can cool neighbourhoods by roughly 2–5°C, cut household cooling energy use and reduce heat-related illness. It calls for scaling them up in informal and heat-vulnerable neighbourhoods.

items.t: Nagpur’s rivers and lakes see huge construction, Rs 200-crore fountains
items.x: This essay shows how Nagpur’s network of lakes and rivers, once its natural cooling system, has been built over and polluted. Satellite data from the 29 May 2024 heat wave showed neighbourhoods near lakes were 4–8°C cooler. It argues that the Futala Lake beautification project, the Supreme Court ruling that it is not a wetland, and fragmented jurisdiction all favour concrete over restoration. The essay calls for ecological restoration, 100 m green belts, and building approvals that protect water bodies, noting that the burden falls hardest on informal and outdoor workers.
